title: Pressure behavior in a roller pump-driven low-flow VACC mock circuit with inactive de-airing pump: A descriptive bench characterization under reduced patient-side effective filling pressure conditions
content:
by Keizo Wauchi, Takahiro Okumura, Keisuke Matsuda, Hiroki Sato, Masahiro Miyata, Kenji Tani

This exploratory bench study characterized pressure behavior in a roller pump-driven low-flow valve-type semi-closed extracorporeal circulation (VACC) mock circuit under experimentally reduced patient-side effective filling pressure conditions with the de-airing pump inactive. Pressures were measured at four sites: circuit-reservoir pressure (Pc), patient-side mock-reservoir outlet pressure (Pv), roller pump inlet pressure (Pi), and roller pump outlet pressure (Po). Pump flow-rate settings were 50–300 mL/min. Circuit-reservoir negative-pressure setpoints were 0, −10, −20, −30, and −40 mmHg, and patient-side mock-reservoir negative-pressure setpoints were 0, −5, and −10 mmHg. A 32 wt% aqueous glycerol solution was used. Pc generally reflected the circuit-reservoir negative-pressure setpoint, with a mean difference of −0.18 mmHg (95% CI, −0.37 to 0.00). The 95% CIs summarize variability among technical replicates within this bench system and should not be interpreted as population-inferential estimates. Pv decreased stepwise according to the patient-side setpoint. Within the common evaluation range, mean differences versus 0 mmHg were −5.7 mmHg (95% CI, −6.0 to −5.3) for the −5 mmHg condition and −9.2 mmHg (95% CI, −9.5 to −8.9) for the −10 mmHg condition. Pi shifted in the negative direction as the pump flow-rate setting increased, whereas Po increased monotonically under the fixed occluder condition. Delivered flow was independently verified volumetrically before the main experiments at 100, 200, and 300 mL/min but was not continuously measured during the pressure experiments. Therefore, Po was interpreted primarily in relation to the pump flow-rate setting rather than as a directly measured hydraulic pressure–flow relationship. These data provide baseline pressure-characterization information for future mock-circuit studies and do not establish clinical safety, efficacy, or a stable operating range.
